prime.problem: Naive string search slides the pattern one step after every mismatch and re-reads text it has already matched. On inputs like a×99 + b in a×10,000 that is 990,100 comparisons. A search that never backs up in the text needs to know, in advance, how much of a partial match can be reused.
prime.fits: First Strings card. Like the two-pointer scans in Searching, it wins by never moving an index backwards; the price is a precomputed table. Rolling hash and the suffix automaton follow as the other ways to compare substrings.
expect: border: a proper prefix that is also a suffix
prime.goal: Build an lps table by hand, run the search with its fall-backs, and prove the whole thing is O(n + m).

attend: After a mismatch with j characters matched, why is lps[j − 1] exactly how much of the match can be kept?
Why is "the border of a border is a border" what makes the fall-back chain correct?
Why does the C at index 4 of ABABCABAB reset every border to 0?
Why can fall-backs never outnumber the steps forward, so the search is ≤ 2n comparisons?
In Shortest Palindrome, why is the separator # needed, and what goes wrong for aaa without it?

must: After matching p[0..j) the last j text characters are known → the longest border of p[0..j) is the longest prefix of p that could start a new match there → on a mismatch jump to j = lps[j − 1] without moving the text index → the text is read once, left to right

j rises by at most 1 per text character and every fall-back lowers it by at least 1 → total fall-backs ≤ total rises ≤ n → search ≤ 2n comparisons, table ≤ 2m → O(n + m) worst case (19,901 vs naive 990,100 on a×99 + b in a×10,000)

lps on s + # + reverse(s) → its last value is the longest prefix of s equal to a suffix of reverse(s) → that's the longest palindromic prefix → prepend the reverse of the rest (aacecaaa → aaacecaaa); # stops a border from crossing the join
elevated: After a full match set j = lps[m − 1] instead of 0 → overlapping matches are still found
Smallest period of p = m − lps[m − 1] (5 for ABABCABAB) → the table answers repetition questions, not just search
reference: the source's shifted-by-one table form (lps[j + 1], t = lps[t])
the 23 vs 29 comparison counts on the textbook example

compress.prompt: In 3–4 sentences from memory: what lps[j] stores, what the search does on a mismatch and why that's safe, and why the total work is linear.
checklist: lps[j] = length of the longest proper border of p[0..j]
on mismatch: j = lps[j − 1], repeat; the text index stays put
the border is the only part of the match that could begin a new match
j's rises bound its falls, so ≤ 2n comparisons in the search
the same table gives palindromic prefixes and periods

retrieve.q: Explain why KMP never needs to move its text pointer backwards, when naive search restarts at i + 1 after every mismatch.
answer: the characters just matched are a prefix of the pattern, so they're known without re-reading
the lps table says which shorter prefix those characters also end with
resuming at that prefix length continues from the same text position

retrieve.q: Walk through the mismatch at text position 4 (the D) in the card's search, with ABAB matched: every fall-back and comparison until j settles.
answer: D ≠ p[0] = A, j is 0 → move on to the next text character

retrieve.q: You must search one 10 MB log for 5,000 different keywords. Run KMP 5,000 times? What would you use, and why?
answer: 5,000 KMP runs read the text 5,000 times: O(5,000 · n)
Aho–Corasick builds one automaton over all keywords and reads the text once
for many queries of different patterns against one text, a suffix automaton or suffix array built once also fits

compare.q: KMP and Rabin–Karp both run in O(n + m). What does each compare at each step, which design choice gives KMP a worst-case guarantee, and how does each fail?
answer: KMP compares characters, guided by the border table; Rabin–Karp compares window hashes and checks characters on a hit
KMP's bound is deterministic: its pointer argument holds for every input
Rabin–Karp fails on adversarial collisions (known B, p) or many real matches; KMP only answers "where does this one pattern occur", not general substring equality

compare.q: Both KMP and Manacher reuse work instead of re-reading characters. What does each reuse, and what quantity only moves forward in each?
answer: KMP reuses the border of what was just matched; the text index only moves forward
Manacher reuses the mirror's radius inside the rightmost palindrome; its right edge r only moves forward
in both, a monotone pointer bounds the total work by O(n)

predict.q: Search for AABA in AABAACAADAABAABA. Predict the match positions, and whether KMP's comparison count lands nearer 16 (one per text character) or 30.
predict.answer: Matches at 0, 9 and 12 (the last two overlap, found because j falls back to lps[3] = 1 after a full match). KMP makes 20 comparisons: 16 text characters plus 4 fall-backs. Naive search makes 30.

apply.task: Build the lps table for AABAACAABAA step by step (t before, compare, fall back, lps[j]). Then use it to give the pattern's smallest period, and compute Shortest Palindrome for abcd with the s + # + reverse(s) trick.
apply.done: lps = [0, 1, 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; smallest period = 11 − 5 = 6; the glued string's last lps is 1 (only a), so the answer is dcb + abcd = dcbabcd.
apply.hint: At j = 2 (B), t = 1 and p[1] = A ≠ B, so fall back to lps[0] = 0, then B ≠ A: lps[2] = 0.
